title: Idiom Orchard
intro: English is full of expressions that mean nothing literally — piece of cake, cost an arm and a leg, once in a blue moon. Match each one to its real meaning.

A2.right: very easy (The exam was a piece of cake.)
A2.why: Cake is easy to eat, so a “piece of cake” is something very easy.
Just a picture of very heavy rain, like Spanish “llover a cántaros”.
It means a bit unwell, like a cold or a headache, not seriously ill.

A2.right: start a conversation in an awkward situation
A2.why: Ships broke the ice to open a path; you “break the ice” to get people talking.

A2.left: cost an arm and a leg
A2.why: Like Spanish “costar un ojo de la cara”: you pay with a part of your body.
A “blue moon” is a rare extra full moon, so it means almost never.
Informal: you “hit the books” when you start studying seriously, often before an exam.
Not like “estar en las nubes” (daydreaming): on cloud nine means extremely happy.
Blue is the colour of sadness in English, as in “the blues”.

A2.right: a lazy person who watches a lot of TV
A2.why: Someone who sits on the sofa all day, as still as a potato.
Like Spanish “de memoria”: she learnt the poem by heart.
Keep an eye on the paella while I answer the door: watch it so it doesn't burn.

B1.right: decide to do something difficult or unpleasant
B1.why: Legend says soldiers bit a bullet during surgery without anaesthetic: you accept the pain and do it.

B1.left: let the cat out of the bag
B1.why: The secret escapes like a cat from a sack; Spanish says “irse de la lengua”.

B1.left: the ball is in your court
B1.right: it's your decision or turn to act
B1.why: From tennis: the ball is on your side of the court, so now you must act.

B1.right: something that seems bad but turns out good
B1.why: It looks like bad luck at first, but it is really a “blessing” (una bendición).
Once a ball starts rolling, it keeps going: you start the activity.
You decide the working day is over: “Let's call it a day and go home.”

B1.right: said when someone appears just as you're talking about them
B1.why: Short for “speak of the devil and he will appear”; Spanish says “hablando del rey de Roma”.

B1.right: lose the chance to do something
B1.why: If you arrive late, the boat has already gone: the chance is lost.
A cowboy pulls on the reins to stop his horses: slow down, wait a moment.
Spanish “cruzar los dedos” is exactly the same gesture and idea.
Hot water burns, so if you're “in hot water” someone is angry with you.
Sleep first and decide in the morning, like Spanish “consultarlo con la almohada”.

B2.why: Before electricity, working late meant burning oil in a lamp at midnight.

B2.right: do something badly to save time or money
B2.why: Cutting across a corner saves distance but skips steps, so the result is poor.
You go further than the journey requires: more effort than anyone asked for.

B2.right: join something popular because others are doing it
B2.why: In 19th-century America politicians climbed onto the band's wagon at parades to look popular.

B2.right: a lot of fuss about something unimportant
B2.why: A storm too small to matter; Spanish says “una tormenta en un vaso de agua”.
Spanish says “andarse por las ramas”; British English also says “beat about the bush”.
From boxing: the trainer throws the towel into the ring to stop the fight. Spanish “tirar la toalla”.
You find the meaning that isn't written directly, just like Spanish “leer entre líneas”.

B2.left: bite off more than you can chew
B2.right: try to do more than you can manage
B2.why: Take too big a bite and you can't chew it: too many jobs at once.

B2.right: the final problem that makes you lose patience
B2.why: From “the straw that broke the camel's back”; Spanish says “la gota que colma el vaso”.

B2.right: a guess made with little information
B2.why: Like firing a gun at night: you hope to hit something, but you're guessing.

B2.right: pretend not to notice something wrong
B2.why: Nelson put his telescope to his blind eye to ignore an order: deliberately not seeing.

C1.left: take something with a pinch of salt
C1.why: A doubtful story is easier to swallow with a little salt; Spanish says “cogerlo con pinzas”.

C1.right: an obvious problem nobody wants to mention
C1.why: Something as big as an elephant, yet everyone acts as if they can't see it.

C1.right: get to the point without wasting time
C1.why: From old films: skip the boring scenes and go straight to the chase.

C1.right: someone dangerous who seems harmless or friendly
C1.why: From Aesop's fables: danger hidden behind a gentle look. Spanish “lobo con piel de cordero”.
In golf, “par” is the normal score: nothing unusual, sadly expected.

C1.right: only a small visible part of a much bigger problem
C1.why: Most of an iceberg is under water; you only see a small part of the problem.
Like Spanish “echar leña al fuego”: you make the anger or the problem bigger.

C1.left: a leopard can't change its spots
C1.right: people don't fundamentally change their nature
C1.why: A leopard keeps its spots for life, just as people keep their character.

C1.right: a false clue that distracts attention
C1.why: A strong-smelling smoked fish was said to pull hunting dogs off the trail: a misleading clue.

C1.right: take the attention or praise someone else expected
C1.why: An 18th-century playwright invented a stage thunder effect; a rival used it, and he said his thunder was stolen.

C1.left: bite the hand that feeds you
C1.right: harm someone who helps or supports you
C1.why: Like a dog biting its owner: you hurt the very person who looks after you.

C1.left: a taste of your own medicine
C1.right: the same bad treatment you give to others
C1.why: The doctor must swallow the bitter medicine he gives his patients.
